name: Dahalo
catalog_citation: Maddieson, Ian, Sinisa Spajic, Bonny Sands & Peter Ladefoged. 1993. Phonetic structures of Dahalo. UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 84: 25-65. (scan at escholarship.org/uc/item/8k45g432)
catalog_locator: sec. 5 'Suprasegmentals', printed p. 46 (PDF p. 52 of the WPP 84 volume scan)
catalog_quote: 5. Suprasegmentals. Dahalo is a language with pitch accent. Tosco (1991) while admitting that “a lot of work remains to be done in this field” has advanced the understanding of Dahalo tonal processes considerably. In our transcriptions we have assigned each syllable a high (H) or a low (L) tone, marking only the high with an acute accent. The most frequent pattern is for a high tone to fall on the first syllable. Cases where there is more than one high tone on a non-compound word are rare, but all-low words are not unusual. The narrow-band spectrograms provided in Figure 4 enable a few of the tonal properties of the language to be noted. Figure 4c shows a LL word /ʔani/ “head” (11), while 4a shows a HL word /p'úʔʔu/ “pierce” (373). These are the only permitted disyllabic patterns. Generally the low tone immediately following a high shows a rather slow decline of pitch over the syllable.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim on the page image we hold (printed p. 46, sec. 5) of Maddieson et al. 1993. (2) The deciding source is a first-hand instrumental phonetic study by UCLA phoneticians that states outright 'Dahalo is a language with pitch accent', gives culminativity (more than one H per non-compound word 'rare'), permits all-L words, and shows LL vs HL disyllables — so H presence is lexical and no stress rule exists to code; the tonal-OR-pitch accent exit follows directly. (3) The fuller primary, Tosco 1991 (the language's only grammar), is not yet obtained and could not be downloaded (academia.edu/ResearchGate login walls; no archive.org or repository copy), but the WPP authors cite it precisely for 'tonal processes', so nothing suggests it would move the record toward a stress coding; no newer prosodic study exists (ELAR 2025 deposit is undescribed documentation; Mous 2022 on Cushitic tone

sources.quote: No mention of Dahalo. General claim (abstract): Cushitic languages labelled 'pitch accent' 'cannot be considered stress languages because the criterion of obligatoriness of every word having a stressed unit is not valid for them'; in Hyman's typology they are (restricted) tone languages.
